notes.title: Nvidia threw its biggest party ever. The guests are paying later.
body: Nvidia threw the biggest party in its history last night. Revenue for the quarter that ended Oct. 25 was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and about $7.8 billion above the middle of its own forecast. This morning the stock opened higher, then slid. Around 10:40 a.m. Pacific it sat near $152, about 2% below Tuesday's close, while SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, was roughly flat. Record night. Cold morning.

Some context before anyone calls it a flop. Nvidia walked into the print already bruised. It closed Tuesday at $155.46, down 35.02% from its Oct. 6 close. SOXX fell 28.00% over the same stretch. This was also the first report since the board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO on Nov. 11. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches for a successor. The release now mentions an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee. What it covers isn't in any filing, so I'm not guessing.

Plot twist: a lot of the money hasn't arrived yet. Revenue grew $19.6 billion from July. Accounts receivable, the bills customers haven't paid, grew $18.0 billion. Nvidia now waits about 64 days to get paid, up from 60 last quarter. The company gave two reasons. Lots of new Rubin systems shipped late in the quarter. And it offered extended payment terms on big multi-quarter deals with certain investment-grade customers.

Picture a wedding caterer booked solid for a year. The food is great, the guests are thrilled, and the biggest couples now get to pay after the honeymoon. The caterer isn't broke. The caterer is just carrying the bill. Investment-grade means those couples are good for it. It still means Nvidia is fronting the money.

And the fronting isn't only invoices. Nvidia's supply commitments jumped from $279 billion to $390 billion, mostly multi-year memory deals. Its guarantees now add up to $118 billion of maximum exposure. Most of that is up to $105 billion of credit support for an Ohio data center campus that will be leased to OpenAI, phasing in from fiscal 2029. Nvidia says it hasn't paid on any guarantee so far. Its own commentary says many neoclouds and AI labs are growing faster than their balance sheets can support. That's Nvidia saying it, not me.

My take: the business is real, and most of the cash is too. Free cash flow was $43.8 billion, about double July's $21.3 billion. But Nvidia is acting more like a lender than it used to, and lenders get judged on who pays them back. Tempted to grab the AI king at a 35% discount? I get it. The catch: next quarter's $130.0 billion forecast includes an extra week, which flatters the growth. What proves the dip-buyers wrong: payment days climbing again, or a guarantee actually getting called.

One thing to watch: the 10-Q Nvidia says it will file in the coming weeks. If the 64 days was a launch-week hiccup, the next number should shrink. If it's simply how Nvidia sells now, it won't. Filing over feelings.

notes.title: TSMC had its best month ever. Then Washington added a security line.
body: Taiwan Semiconductor showed up to this week holding the best report card of its life. The market walked it to the exit anyway. Over three sessions through Monday, TSM fell 9.65% and closed at $373.45. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, fell 9.12% over the same stretch. Best month ever, three red days in a row. I love a contradiction.

Start with the receipt. On Nov. 10, TSMC said October revenue was about NT$586.89 billion. That's up 14.7% from September and up 59.7% from a year earlier, and it's the biggest month the company has posted. TSMC is the factory. Companies like Nvidia draw the chip, and TSMC builds it. When its register rings like that, somebody is still ordering.

Plot twist: on Monday the Commerce Department released a new export rule, and TSMC's job title is in it. It's an interim final rule, which means it's real, not a proposal. It takes effect once it's published in the Federal Register, and the public gets 60 days to comment after that. The headline part is about rentals. Washington's worry is that companies based in China, which can't freely buy America's best AI chips, rent time on them in data centers abroad. The rule goes after that. It also requires a license to ship advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, with an exception for US-based companies that file reports.

The part I circled is third on the list. Chip factories and packagers already have to assume certain advanced chips are restricted unless the customer clears a checklist. The new rule removes some of the ways to clear it when the chip designer, or its parent company, sits in a restricted country. Commerce says foreign foundries must do "robust due diligence" on who really owns the customer. Foundry means contract chip factory. That's TSMC.

Picture an airline that just sold more seats than ever. Then security adds a second line and tells the airline to check who really paid for each ticket. The flights still go. Boarding gets slower, and some passengers don't get on. Nobody at the gate can say how many yet.

Here's why I'm not pinning the whole drop on the rule. Monday was ugly for everyone. SOXX lost 5.41% in one day and TSM lost 6.34%. Nvidia, a major TSMC customer, reports after the close tonight, its first report since Jensen Huang's exit as CEO last week. That's a lot of nerves in one room. But by late Tuesday morning Pacific time, TSM was down about 4% more while SOXX was down about 1%. Monday it fell with the pack. Today it's out in front. My read: that gap is the rule.

My take: this is a paperwork problem until someone proves it's a revenue problem. TSMC's guide for this quarter, $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion in revenue, came out Oct. 15. That was a month before this rule existed, so the guide doesn't know about it. Tempted to buy a record month on sale? I get it. The catch is that nobody has priced the new security line. What proves the dip-buyers wrong: TSMC trimming that guide, or saying orders got delayed by the checks.
One thing to watch: TSMC's November revenue, due around Dec. 10. If the register keeps ringing after the rule kicks in, the line was just a line. Filing over feelings.

notes.title: Micron dumped its consumer brand. Now a judge brought it up in court.
body: Last week Micron had a glow-up. Over five sessions through Friday, the stock rose 12.80% and closed at $778.31. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, rose 9.35% over the same stretch. Memory got the good table again. Then the weekend delivered a court date.

Here are the plain facts. In an order dated Nov. 14, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise in Northern California refused to throw out a class action against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. Seventeen consumers and small businesses filed it in June. They allege the three agreed to squeeze the supply of ordinary DRAM, the memory inside laptops, phones and servers, while moving factory space to HBM, the stacked memory that AI chips run on. The companies deny it and argued that market conditions drove their choices. Nothing is proven. The ruling only says the complaint is detailed enough to keep going.

Plot twist: one of the receipts the court leaned on is Micron's own. In December 2025, Micron said it would exit Crucial, its consumer memory brand, and stop shipping to that channel by February. Micron framed it as freeing up supply for bigger, faster-growing customers. The order treated moves like that, which are hard to undo, plus near-identical customer screening questions all three adopted in January, as support for a plausible conspiracy. The judge wrote that the allegations go beyond "hawks flying in formation." Translation: birds can fly the same way for their own reasons. These three allegedly compared flight plans.

Picture the only three clubs on the block killing general admission in the same month and keeping just the bottle-service line. Maybe each owner did the math alone. Maybe there was a group chat. The judge isn't saying there was a group chat. She's saying it's fair to ask for the phones. That part has a name: discovery.

This crowd also has an ex the court remembers. Samsung and Hynix paid fines over a DRAM price-fixing cartel that ran from 1998 to 2002, and Micron got immunity for cooperating. A later suit over supply cuts in 2016 to 2018 was tossed, and an appeals court agreed in 2022. The companies said this case was a rerun. The judge said the new details make it a different show.

Now the tape. By late Monday morning Pacific time, Micron traded about 7% below Friday's close, and SOXX was down about 5%. My read: the gavel isn't the whole story. The entire chip aisle is red, with Nvidia's report due Tuesday. Pinning one red Monday on one court order is how you end up wrong twice.

My take: the money risk here is slow, not sudden. The awkward part is a word Wall Street loved. Memory makers have pitched investors on supply discipline, meaning no more overbuilding, and investors paid up for it. The court called those investor comments neutral on their own. But the more that discipline looks like a team sport, the more expensive the story gets. Tempted to call this dip just a lawsuit? Fair. What proves that wrong is evidence of coordination coming out in discovery, or a settlement big enough to dent the cash flow.
One thing to watch: Dec. 7, when all three must formally answer the complaint. I want to see how Micron explains the Crucial exit in its own words. Filing over feelings.

notes.title: Nvidia lost its CEO. The rest of the chip squad kept partying.
body: Last week the chip crowd threw a comeback party. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, rose 9.35% over five sessions through Friday. Nvidia, the guest of honor, fell 12.75% over the same stretch and closed Friday at $162.85. Per Yahoo Finance, its market value slipped back under $4 trillion. Everybody else danced. Nvidia stood by the coat check.

Here's the part that isn't gossip. On Thursday, Nvidia said Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and left the board, effective immediately. The filing gave no reason. Press coverage tied the exit to his personal relationships, including one with a woman who, per The New York Times, U.S. surveillance suggested was passing information to Beijing. On Nov. 8, the board opened an independent investigation and said it had no reason to think company secrets were compromised. No findings are public yet. That's a serious story about real people, so I'm keeping it plain.

The stock part, though, is pure tabloid. Thursday it dropped as much as 14% at the open, per Yahoo Finance, then clawed most of it back to close down 4.34%. Small investors piled in fast: Vanda Research counted a net $111 million of retail buying in the first 30 minutes. Friday, the stock slid another 2.01%. The dip-buyers showed up for the bounce. The bounce left early.

Plot twist: the company didn't stop. Colette Kress, the finance chief, is now interim CEO and keeps the CFO job too. Harvey Jones became Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The board is searching for a permanent CEO, inside and outside the company. And the earnings date didn't budge: results land Tuesday, Nov. 17, after the close. The board says operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap continue “without interruption.” In fantasy-league terms, the head coach is gone mid-season, but the roster on the field is the same players. My read: Tuesday's numbers cover a quarter that already happened. A coaching change can't rewrite them.

So who has the leverage now? The customers. For years, part of the Nvidia pitch was the founder on stage with the roadmap in his head. Now the person holding the clicker is the same person who signs the checks. My read: the guide, meaning management's forecast for next quarter, matters more than the quarter itself. It's the first number this new lineup owns. If buyers were getting cold feet, that's where it would show up first.

I get the itch. The biggest name in chips, down hard in a week its friends rallied, and your thumb is hovering like it spotted a star on the waiver wire nobody claimed. The catch: buying here is a bet that the business never needed one person to sell it. If Tuesday's guide comes in soft, or a customer pushes a delivery date, that bet is wrong. And the investigation findings are still a blank page.

One thing on my calendar: Tuesday's forecast for next quarter. Last Monday I asked whether any customer actually moved a delivery date. I'm still asking. If the guide holds up and nobody moves a date, the roster carried the team. If it slips, the coach mattered more than the depth chart said.

notes.title: Cerebras finally turned a profit. Its own scorecard did the counting.
body: Friday, the chip crowd had a rough night out. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, fell 3.67%. Meanwhile Cerebras was dancing on the table. The stock closed up 11.22% at $108.72. At its best moment of the day it was up about 23%. So it left half the party before last call.

Quick intro. Cerebras builds one enormous chip out of a whole silicon wafer, then rents out its speed through its own cloud. It went public in May at $185 a share. By Thursday's close it was down about 47% from there. Not exactly a debut season.

Then the report. The headline: a profit. $29.8 million, where a year ago there was a loss. Revenue up 70% to $230.9 million. Cloud revenue more than tripled. The full-year forecast went up to $940 to $960 million, from $880 to $890 million. And per Reuters, the company said it signed a cloud deal with Microsoft, with details coming next year.

Plot twist. Every one of those numbers wears the word “core.” That's Cerebras' own scorecard. The official version, under standard accounting rules, tells a different story. Revenue was $210.8 million. The company lost $161.2 million, or 67 cents a share. The gap is mostly two things. Stock paid to employees: $155.1 million this quarter, up from $11.3 million a year ago. And $36.4 million knocked off revenue for warrants it gave customers, meaning rights to buy Cerebras shares at a set price. Core versus official is the dating-profile photo versus the first date. Same person. Better lighting.

My read: the core story is real, and the official story shows who's paying for it. Shareholders are covering staff pay in stock, and customers got equity sweeteners to sign. That works while the cash pile is this big. Cerebras had $3.07 billion in cash at the end of September, and $7.8 billion counting restricted cash and short-term investments. It also has $26.1 billion of contracted work it hasn't delivered yet. Orders aren't the bottleneck. Per Reuters, the CEO blamed delivery delays on shortages of land and power. Everybody in AI is waiting on the electrician.

One more side-eye. On the official count, hardware sales, the actual systems, fell to $68.9 million from $96.8 million a year ago. Cerebras is selling fewer boxes and renting out more speed. Fine business if the cloud stays full. Expensive while it builds the space to hold it.

I get the itch. A stock still about 41% under its IPO price, a profit headline, a Microsoft name-drop, and your thumb is twitching. Friday already showed you the catch. It ran about 23%, then closed at 11. Buyers took the headline. Sellers read the footnotes. Buying here is a bet that the core numbers turn into the official numbers before the stock-pay bill grows. If that gap keeps widening, the bet is wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the fourth-quarter report. Cerebras guided core revenue to $310 to $330 million. If it lands at $310 million or more and the official loss shrinks, the glow-up is real. If core revenue misses the low end, this profit was a one-night stand, and my read was wrong.

notes.title: Applied Materials guided to a record. It needed an extra week to get there.
body: Thursday night, Applied Materials strutted out of earnings with a record in one hand and a forecast in the other. Friday morning, the paparazzi caught it slipping. By late morning the stock was near $365, down about 4%. Before anyone calls it a breakup, look around the room. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, was down about the same. The session isn't over, so that's a snapshot, not a receipt.

Quick intro for the new kids. Applied doesn't make chips. It makes the machines that make chips: the tools that lay down, carve and polish the layers on a silicon wafer. Last quarter, revenue was $10.41 billion, up 53% from a year ago. The fiscal year came in at $34.45 billion. Everyone building AI factories needs these machines, and Applied is the one selling them.

Plot twist. Then came the guide, meaning management's forecast for next quarter: $11.1 billion, give or take $500 million. A record. Except on the call, the finance chief said it's a 14-week quarter. The one that just ended had 13. Split it per week and the new guide lands about 1% below what Applied just did. That's my math, not theirs. It's like bragging about your biggest Spotify Wrapped ever in a leap year. Technically true. You also had an extra day.

So is the glow-up fake? My read: no. On the call, the finance chief said clean room capacity “remains a gating factor,” and that “our Q1 number would be slightly higher if everything were perfectly available.” A clean room is the dust-free building where these machines get installed. Translation: customers want more tools than there are rooms to plug them into. And they're paying early. Contract liabilities, money customers paid before getting everything they ordered, hit $3.59 billion, up from $2.57 billion a year ago. Inventory climbed to $6.89 billion. That looks like a company stocking up to ship, not one waiting by the phone.

Here's who has the leverage. When buyers prepay and the bottleneck is buildings, the toolmaker isn't the one begging. CEO Gary Dickerson said the company's current view is that demand for chipmaking equipment rises more than 30% next year. Applied also spent $2 billion buying back its own stock last quarter. Looks like management likes the order book enough to bet its own cash on it.

One side-eye. China was 25% of revenue last quarter, down from 29% a year earlier, and the finance chief said shipments there will probably be under 25% of the business in 2027. Losing share with your biggest out-of-town customer is fine while everyone else is lining up. It's less fine if that line gets shorter.

I get the itch. A record quarter, a red morning, and your thumb is hovering over the buy button like it just got a restock alert. The catch: on Thursday the stock already slid 3.58% into the report while SOXX barely moved, so some of the doubt was priced in before anyone read a word. Buying this dip is a bet that the extra week is calendar noise, not makeup over slowing demand.

One thing on my calendar: Applied's February guide, for a normal 13-week quarter. If it's $11.1 billion or higher, this week's wobble was a calendar hiccup. If it comes in below that, the extra week was doing the heavy lifting, and my read was wrong.

notes.title: Nebius cashed a one-time bonus. Then it retired the scoreboard.
body: Wednesday, Nebius strutted into earnings like it already knew the verdict. The stock closed up 15.44%, at $154.69, the day after CoreWeave reported. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, rose 6.01%. Then Thursday morning the report landed, and by late morning the stock was trading near $130. The session isn't over, so that's a snapshot, not a receipt.

Quick intro for the new kids. Nebius rents out AI computers. It fills data centers with Nvidia chips and leases the horsepower to people building AI. Third-quarter revenue was $980.8 million, up 571% from a year ago and up 68% from the second quarter. On the red carpet, that's a full glow-up.

Plot twist. In its shareholder letter, Nebius says about $325 million of that was non-recurring revenue, tied to what it calls its asset-light model. One-time money. Take it out and the quarter is roughly $656 million. Against $582.3 million in the second quarter, that's growth of about 13%. Still growth. Just not the 68% on the poster.

Same letter, one more line: “We no longer see ARR as the right measure of our business.” ARR means annual recurring revenue, the yearly pace of repeat sales, and it was the number this crowd lived by. It's like landing a one-time bonus, letting everyone think it's your salary, then announcing salary isn't a useful number anymore. Maybe there's a good reason. The timing is still the gossip. Nebius also now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3.0 to $3.4 billion range.

Now the cash. Operating cash flow, the money the business actually brought in, was negative $273 million. Last quarter it was positive $2.25 billion. By the end of September, customers owed Nebius about $4.04 billion. My read: big prepaid deals got billed, but the checks hadn't cleared yet. Meanwhile it spent $7.3 billion on equipment in three months.

Here's the part I'll defend. The letter says prepayments on deals signed in the third quarter covered more than 100% of the related equipment spending. For 2027, it guides revenue of $12 to $13 billion and capital spending of $40 to $45 billion, with 75% to 85% of that covered by customer prepayments and loans backed by the gear. Pre-tax breakeven is pegged for the fourth quarter of 2027. So the customers are also the bank. That's leverage. It's also concentration: if a big tenant pays late, the landlord feels it fast.

I get the itch. A hot stock gives back a chunk in one morning, and your thumb starts calling it a markdown. The catch: buying here is a bet that those invoices turn into cash on schedule. If next quarter's operating cash flow is still negative, that bet is wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the next quarterly report. I want operating cash flow back above zero and that receivables pile shrinking. A bonus is nice. A paycheck that shows up every month is the business.

notes.title: CoreWeave sold out the tour. The fans are paying for the stage.
body: Tuesday night, CoreWeave walked into earnings looking like it slept in its car. The stock had dropped 9.32% in five sessions, to $48.73. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, fell 5.43% over the same stretch. CNBC put the one-month slide near 40%. Then the numbers hit, and Wednesday morning it opened near $56. The session isn’t over, so that’s a snapshot, not a receipt.

Quick intro for the new kids. CoreWeave rents out AI computers. It fills data centers with Nvidia chips and leases the horsepower to AI labs. Last quarter, revenue was $3.661 billion, up 168% from a year ago. It raised its full-year sales target to $13.0 to $13.3 billion. And the backlog, meaning signed contracts it hasn’t delivered yet, hit about $132.5 billion. That’s a tour sold out for years.

Plot twist. The sold-out tour still lost money. The business earned $207 million in operating income, which is profit before interest and taxes. Interest on its debt cost $846 million. That’s four times what the show cleared at the door. Net loss: $709 million. The band is packing arenas, and the loan on the tour bus is eating the merch table.

And the loans are getting pricey. CNBC reported that some CoreWeave bonds recently yielded more than 16%, and that the finance chief told analysts the company doesn’t plan to sell more of that kind of debt through 2027 at those rates. So who pays for the next stage? CEO Michael Intrator said it in the release: “approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone.” Read that again. The fans are fronting the cash for the venue.

My read: that’s the real headline. When lenders want 16% and customers hand over deposits instead, the customers need the computers more than CoreWeave needs the bond market. That’s leverage, the good kind. It also means the same AI labs are now the tenant and the bank. If one of them slows down, both doors close at once.

I get the itch. A beaten-up stock jumps on a record quarter and your thumb starts doing math. The catch: capital spending, the money going into chips and buildings, is guided to $37 to $39 billion this year. That’s nearly three times the sales target. The company also told us interest runs $1.05 to $1.15 billion next quarter. Chasing the pop is a bet that the deposits keep showing up faster than the bills. If the prepayments come in light, that bet is wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the next quarterly report. I want to see that $9 billion actually land on the balance sheet. A sold-out tour is a promise. A deposit is a receipt. I’ll clap for the encore when the check clears.

notes.title: Google built its own lock. Then it called AMD.
body: Monday, the chip crowd limped back from a brutal week. AMD walked in with a fresh haircut and a story to tell. The stock closed up 13.26%, at $508.58. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, rose 7.49%. Same session, nearly double the group’s bounce.

The story landed before the opening bell. AMD said its fifth-generation EPYC processors run the host side of Google Cloud’s new TPU 8tx. A TPU is Google’s own AI chip. The host CPU is the stage manager: it schedules the work, preps the data and keeps the TPUs fed. Google Cloud’s Mark Lohmeyer said the pairing brings hardware-enforced confidential computing to Cloud TPUs for the first time. In normal words, the data stays locked even while the machine is working on it. Model weights, prompts, the whole diary.

Plot twist. Google already makes its own server CPU. It’s called Axion, it’s Arm-based, and Google has run it alongside its recent TPUs so it leans less on outside chip vendors. So this is the homeowner who designed a custom lock, then handed the neighbor the spare key to the safe room. My read: when the job was security, Google decided the neighbor’s deadbolt was better. That’s a real compliment from a company that would love to need nobody.

Now rewind to Thursday. AMD fell 17.26% in one session, to $404.40, when the market dumped anything tied to AI data centers. Two sessions later, it closed 4.05% above Wednesday’s close. SOXX is still 2.25% under it. The rest of the class is icing its ankles. AMD is already running laps. Oppenheimer also upgraded the stock Monday, per Yahoo Finance’s recap, so the press release showed up with a hype man.

Here are the receipts I don’t have. Neither company put a dollar figure on this. No chip count. No price. No date for general availability, which is when any customer can actually rent the thing. This is a seating chart, not an invoice. A 13% day is a lot of applause for an announcement that hasn’t billed anyone yet.

I get the itch. The stock took a punch, got up swinging, and your thumb wants in like it’s a limited drop. The catch: buying after a 13% day means paying Monday’s price for news that may not show up in revenue for a while. And if Google’s next TPU quietly ships with Axion as the host, the chosen-one story gets a lot shorter. That’s what would prove the hype wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the day Google posts TPU 8tx pricing and a general-availability date. That’s when a press release turns into a bill. Until then, AMD has the spare key. I want to see who actually moves in.

notes.title: Nvidia ghosted the rally. The board has questions.
body: Monday’s market showed up to the party in sequins. Nvidia showed up in sunglasses, parked itself by the snack table and refused to dance. The index went green. The chip king went red. When the most popular kid skips the group photo, people start texting.

Here’s what we actually know. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board said it opened an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Same statement, same breath: the board has no reason to think company secrets or national security were compromised. That’s corporate for “we’re checking the locks, nothing looks missing, please stop ringing the doorbell.” Cute. I’ll stop ringing when I see what the locksmith finds.

Also, this was not Nvidia’s first bad night out this week. Stocks partied after the midterms. Then Thursday flipped the lights on at 2 a.m. The Nasdaq fell 5.5%. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, fell 12.15%. The worry: after Democrats won, new data centers could catch more fights over permits and power bills. That’s a fear about future fights, not a new law. But a GPU can write your wedding toast in nine languages and still can’t get the zoning board to text back. No building, no rack. No rack, no delivery.

Plot twist the timeline missed: Nvidia actually held up better than its friends. Five sessions through Nov. 6, Nvidia fell 8.8%. The chip fund fell 13.13%. Not a trophy. Still a receipt. Thursday was the whole squad getting dragged out of the club together. Monday was Nvidia doing the walk of shame alone while everyone else went to brunch. That’s when the board story earns its own headline. The chart shows me the split. It can’t tell me how much is scandal and how much is leftover hangover.

Now, the dip. I see you. It’s down, it’s Nvidia, and your thumb is hovering over buy like it’s hovering over an ex’s new story at 1 a.m. Very human. Also how people end up apologizing over coffee. Before I touch it, I want one receipt. Customers pushing deliveries? Show me dates. Shipping on time but getting paid slower? Show me the cash. Other chip names sliding again? Then it’s a group-chat problem, not an Nvidia scandal.

Because there’s a canyon between a customer saying “take the chips in March instead” and an investor whispering “what if they take the chips in March instead?” One moves real revenue out of the quarter. The other just moves the stock, before a single order changes. If someone swears a delay is real, ask for the project name and the date. Rumors never bring those. Receipts always do.

Nvidia reports Nov. 17, and I’ll be in the front row. Two questions. What did the board find? And did any customer actually move a delivery date? Until then, the chart gets one browser tab and the receipts get another. Yes, I have too many tabs. These two pay rent.
